profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a business school research center between the lead faculty member and the research operations manager for a forthcoming white paper and executive webinar based on a literature review of IT-dependent strategic initiatives and sustained competitive advantage. The center wants to turn the academic review into a practitioner-facing research product for corporate partners before the annual digital strategy forum. The agenda is to decide what the deliverable package includes, how the literature evidence will be organized, who will do each part, and the timeline for producing a draft, internal review, and final release. The expected outcome is a shared plan for assembling the evidence base, drafting the synthesis, preparing figures and examples, and scheduling review milestones.

members.name: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
members.expertise: Strategic information systems, literature synthesis, theory development
members.background: An associate professor who has led several interdisciplinary review projects translating academic research into executive education materials; trained in information systems and strategic management.
members.private_state: She wants the white paper to preserve the conceptual nuance of the original literature so it can later be expanded into a journal-oriented article, and she is concerned that oversimplification for practitioners will make the work feel shallow to academic colleagues.
hidden_assumptions: A 'draft' means a substantively complete narrative with argumentation, citations, and at least rough visuals already embedded so faculty can assess the intellectual contribution.
The 'coding framework' should capture barrier-to-erosion constructs and how they develop over time at the article level, not just descriptive metadata for each source.
Using 'cases' in the practitioner version means short published company examples added after the literature synthesis is stable, not a parallel evidence stream that reshapes the framework.
The 'partner review' step is for light relevance feedback after the internal academic review, because conceptual framing should already be settled before external eyes see it.

members.name: Ethan Cole
members.expertise: Knowledge product delivery, executive-facing research briefs, publication workflows
members.background: A former management consulting research manager who now oversees timelines, analyst coordination, and sponsor-facing outputs for the center's applied research projects.
members.private_state: He wants to hit the forum deadline with a polished sponsor-ready product and avoid late-cycle rewrites, and he is worried that an academically ambitious process will consume analyst time and slip production.
hidden_assumptions: A 'draft' means a publication-shaped document with section headings, key messages, placeholder evidence, and clean formatting that can move into design quickly even if the prose is not final.

The 'coding framework' should be a spreadsheet schema analysts can apply consistently across articles to extract practical fields like industry, initiative type, barrier category, and executive takeaway.
Using 'cases' means selecting 4-6 company examples early so they anchor the storyline and slide deck from the beginning.
The 'partner review' is the standard sponsor checkpoint before internal sign-off, because practical framing and tone should be calibrated early enough to avoid redesign.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have 'a full draft' ready in two weeks.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'full draft' means a near-complete substantive manuscript: integrated argument, literature-based claims, citations, and provisional figures detailed enough for intellectual review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'full draft' means a production-ready shell: formatted document, major sections filled, headline insights stated, and some evidence placeholders sufficient for workflow and design planning.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to using 'full draft' as a normal milestone term, and in competent planning meetings it sounds concrete enough that neither feels a need to unpack the level of completeness implied.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on 'setting up the coding framework' before analysts begin reviewing articles.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means building a theory-informed coding protocol that captures constructs, relationships, and temporal mechanisms from each paper so the synthesis can explain how sustainability develops.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means creating an operational extraction template analysts can use quickly and consistently to populate a comparative database for charts, summaries, and examples.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'coding framework' is standard in evidence-synthesis work and suggests methodological agreement, while the deeper difference lies in whether the tool is designed for conceptual interpretation or production efficiency.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the paper should 'include a few cases' to make the review concrete.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes cases are short illustrative vignettes appended late in the process, drawn from well-known published examples and clearly subordinate to the literature review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes cases include early-selected company mini-profiles that will shape the structure of the paper, webinar narrative, and possibly require analyst research beyond the reviewed articles.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both support adding cases for accessibility, and the phrase sounds like a minor embellishment; the hidden divergence is about whether cases are lightweight illustrations or a broader workstream influencing scope and sequencing.

misalignment_points.topic: Timing and purpose of partner review
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to send it for 'partner review' before finalizing.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that internal faculty review happens first and that partner review is a late-stage external relevance check on a basically finished intellectual product.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that partner review is the normal midpoint sponsor checkpoint used before internal sign-off so audience fit can shape the product before polishing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have institutional experience where 'partner review' is routine, but from different workflows; because each assumes the sequence is already standard, neither thinks to restate what comes before or after it.

turns.inner_thought: We need to preserve the intellectual spine of the literature review even if the output is practitioner-facing. If this becomes too simplified, it will be hard to build it back into a serious article later. The forum matters, but the paper has to show a real synthesis of how IT-dependent initiatives remain defensible over time.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want us to use this meeting to get very clear on how we turn the review on IT-dependent strategic initiatives and sustained advantage into a practitioner-facing white paper and webinar for the forum. If we do it well, it should be accessible for partners without losing the core insight from the literature.

turns.inner_thought: Good, same overall goal. I need a sequence that gets us to a sponsor-ready product on time: paper, webinar deck, design, and the standard checkpoint rhythm. We should build in partner review early enough that we don't get blindsided on tone or relevance after layout starts.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I think the easiest way to manage it is to work backward from the forum date and lock the sequence now—paper first, then the webinar materials, with the review checkpoints built in so nothing bunches up at the end.

turns.inner_thought: Before analysts touch the articles, we need a real coding protocol that captures the four barriers to erosion, the relationships among them, and how those mechanisms unfold over time in each paper. Otherwise we'll end up with a bibliography, not a synthesis.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. For me, the first step is setting up the coding framework before analysts begin reviewing articles, especially so we can capture the four barriers to erosion and how those mechanisms evolve across the literature.

turns.inner_thought: Yes—get the spreadsheet schema defined this week so analysts can code consistently and we can sort the evidence into something usable for charts, summaries, and executive-friendly takeaways. If we overcomplicate it, the team will slow down.
turns.utterance: Agreed. If we set up the coding framework this week, I can have the analysts start with fields that let us sort the articles cleanly by initiative type, industry context, barrier category, and takeaway for executives.

turns.inner_thought: Once the article-level synthesis is underway, I can shape the argument. The cases should come in afterward as brief illustrations from published examples, not as something that drives the framework itself.
turns.utterance: Good. Once the coding is underway, I’d like to start shaping the integrative argument, and then we can include a few cases to make the concepts more tangible for partner companies.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—let's identify four to six company examples early so they anchor the story and give the webinar some concrete narrative. The analysts can gather material in parallel and use those cases to keep the paper grounded.
turns.utterance: Yes, I’m with you on including a few cases. It would help if we identify the likely companies early so the analysts can gather material that supports the storyline and the webinar examples as they go.

turns.inner_thought: Two weeks should be enough to get to a substantively complete manuscript if the coding moves quickly: argument, citations, and rough figures embedded so I can judge whether the framework really explains sustained defensibility. I do not want a shell with bullets.
turns.utterance: In terms of timing, could we aim for a full draft in two weeks? That would give me a chance to review whether the framework is clearly explaining why some IT-dependent initiatives remain defensible over time.

turns.inner_thought: Two weeks for a full draft is workable if that means a publication-shaped document with the sections in place, key messages visible, and enough content for design planning. That still leaves room for cleanup, formatting, and the next checkpoint before we finalize.
turns.utterance: Two weeks works for a full draft. If we hit that, we should still have enough time for layout cleanup, design prep, and the next review stage without putting the forum timeline at risk.

turns.inner_thought: I'll own the substantive synthesis and make sure the framework reflects the literature. Ethan can manage the analysts on coding and collect example material in the background. As long as the cases remain supportive, that division should work.
turns.utterance: Why don’t I take the lead on the synthesis narrative, and you coordinate the analyst support for the article coding and the collection of example material? That should let us move the evidence base and the writing forward at the same time.

turns.inner_thought: Great. Once the draft is assembled, we should send it for partner review as the usual sponsor checkpoint, then make the practical framing adjustments before internal sign-off and final production. Better to calibrate early than redo a polished piece.
turns.utterance: That works. Then once the draft is assembled, we can send it for partner review and fold those comments into the polished version before final release.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, after we've reviewed it internally, partner feedback can confirm relevance and examples without reopening the conceptual structure. As long as the framework is already settled, that step should be useful rather than disruptive.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Feedback at that stage should help confirm that the piece feels relevant and usable without derailing the underlying framework.

turns.inner_thought: Good—we have enough to run with. I'll move on the coding framework this week, start case identification alongside the review, target the draft in two weeks, and slot partner review right after so we stay on production schedule.
turns.utterance: Great, let me recap so we’re aligned: we’ll get the coding framework set up this week, identify a few cases alongside the analyst review, aim for a full draft in two weeks, and then send it for partner review before we finalize.
